Pulumi has less community support because it is less popular. You can get similar results with raw Terraform, which has more documented examples and known workarounds. "I wanted to find Pulumi more useful than I really did."

A user of both in depth: CDK wraps CloudFormation (AWS only, static templates). Pulumi is closer to Terraform but lets you access values available only during execution. Its Automation API lets you code infrastructure migrations. Liked Pulumi's resource model, docs, and team responsiveness, but uses CDK now because of costs.

Pulumi is more like Terraform without HCL: you use a real language to build resources and Pulumi provisions them and manages state. "Much more like Terraform without the handcuffs of HCL. (sometimes handcuffs are useful tho..)"
Pulumi is arguably a leaky abstraction on top of Terraform, which is itself a leaky abstraction on the provider's API. Still, I'm much happier using Pulumi than HCL.

I like it, but everyone I pitched it to said "Ewww, TypeScript for Infra." Pulumi used deprecated Azure stuff for months without fixing it, so you're always late compared to plain Terraform. You also need an account with them.

I used to love Pulumi; managing infra and k8s resources with TypeScript's type system is really nice. But support responsiveness via Slack and GitHub issues has been poor enough that I'm strongly considering removing it from our team's tooling.
It worked really well when I used it with Python. I wish they supported Ruby and had better docs for the Python client.
We switched from Terraform to Pulumi for a new project because one tool handles both cloud infrastructure and k8s configuration, including cleanly deleting k8s resources when config is removed.

I deal with a 40k-line Terraform codebase. The migration paths in Pulumi's docs are completely intractable at this size. tf2pulumi just spits out a single stream to stdout, which won't work for large multi-module projects.
Switched from nixops to Pulumi and found it much easier to use.
Commenter points out that per Pulumi's docs, self-hosting is only available with the Pulumi Enterprise Edition.

Using Pulumi for about a year to manage GCP and AWS environments (5+, each deployment around 500 resources). It was buggy at the beginning, but I've seen a lot of improvement since they started adding typing.
Our org basically banned anything but Terraform "because standardization," so the first barrier is the lack of an HCL-to-Pulumi migration path. The next big stumbling block is the license.

I really liked Pulumi, but it became too complex after a short while. Because all infra resources are defined as code, you end up defining them procedurally (Python) and struggle to arrange and resolve dependencies.
I'm in love with Pulumi, simply one of the best tools in my stack. After about a year I cannot go back to editing YAML files or clicking things in a web UI.

Using Pulumi for a few months with no prior IaC experience: I love it. Its documentation has downsides, mostly around limits on resource name lengths. All our microservices have Pulumi in the CI/CD pipeline; it's extremely powerful.
Last time I checked, Pulumi only worked by calling in to the mothership, so you couldn't build an airgapped infrastructure with it. That was very off-putting and I gave up on Pulumi.

A couple of years ago: a Pulumi run has two phases, building the resource DAG and then applying changes. Values like a subnet ID are effectively futures, so you can't write e.g. 'if my_subnet.id == ...'. Using them required pushing source code to be eval'ed in the second phase.
Twice I've tried to love Pulumi but wound up going back to Terraform, because the Terraform provider docs put clear usage examples front and center.

We tried Pulumi in private beta and are very happy so far. Having used a variety of tools in the space, this is the first time an engineer ever told me: "I really like it, I hope we can keep using it."
